**Step 2 — factorise top and bottom.**
numerator: x⁵(x − 1)
denominator: x³(x − 1)
**Step 3 — cancel.** The common factor **(x − 1)** disappears, and x³ cancels into x⁵:
= x⁵/x³ = **x²**
So the formidable-looking integrand is simply x².
**Step 4 — integrate.**
∫ x² dx = **x³/3** + c ✓
The whole question is the identity in step 1, and once it is applied the integral is the

This is the **king's property** in its most familiar form:
**∫₀^a f(x) dx = ∫₀^a f(a − x) dx**
with a = π/2, where the substitution swaps sine and cosine.
**Step 1 — call the integral I.**
I = ∫₀^(π/2) sin¹⁰⁰⁰x / (sin¹⁰⁰⁰x + cos¹⁰⁰⁰x) dx
**Step 2 — replace x by π/2 − x.** Since sin(π/2 − x) = cos x and cos(π/2 − x) = sin x:
I = ∫₀^(π/2) cos¹⁰⁰⁰x / (cos¹⁰⁰⁰x + sin¹⁰⁰⁰x) dx
The **denominator is unchanged**, being symmetric in the two — which is exactly what makes
the trick work.
**Step 3 — add the two expressions for I.**
2I = ∫₀^(π/2) [sin¹⁰⁰⁰x + cos¹⁰⁰⁰x] / [sin¹⁰⁰⁰x + cos¹⁰⁰⁰x] dx
The integrand is identically **1**:
2I = ∫₀^(π/2) dx = **π/2**
**Step 4 — divide.**
**I = π/4** ✓
The exponent **1000 plays no part whatever** — it is there purely to make the integral look
impossible. Any exponent n gives the same answer, as does any function in place of sinⁿ, so
long as the denominator is the sum of that function and its complement.
The general result: **∫₀^(π/2) f(sin x)/[f(sin x) + f(cos x)] dx = π/4** for any f.
The trap is option (c), π/2 — the value of 2I rather than I.
∴ π/4.

= eᵘ · u + c
